Unit 2 · Chapter 1 · American Imperialism

The Philippine American War: Watch & Read

1898 to 1902

In 1898 the United States took an overseas empire off Spain. In the Philippines, Filipinos believed they had just won their independence and were about to run their own country. In America, the argument over what to do with the islands was only starting.

To the imperialists, the Philippines were the key to a new American empire, a foothold that would carry US influence and US commerce into Asia. To the anti-imperialists, the United States was turning into a brutal imperial master, the exact thing it had said it went to war to fight.

What Happened

Three years, in three parts. The rail beside the next section has the dates.

Allies

May to August 1898

Commodore Dewey destroyed the Spanish fleet in Manila Bay in a single morning, and the United States brought Emilio Aguinaldo back from exile to fight alongside it. Filipino forces took the countryside and surrounded Manila. In June they declared independence and built a republic at Malolos with a constitution and a congress. In August the Spanish garrison surrendered the city to the Americans in a battle arranged in advance, and Filipino troops were kept outside the walls while it happened.

The turn

December 1898 to February 1899

At Paris in December, Spain sold the Philippines to the United States for twenty million dollars. No Filipino was in the room. McKinley ordered American rule extended over every island and called it benevolent assimilation. Aguinaldo answered that his government would not accept it. On the fourth of February an American sentry outside Manila fired on Filipino soldiers, and within a day the two armies that had just beaten Spain together were fighting each other.

The long war

1899 to 1902

For a year the Filipino army fought in the open and lost almost every time. Late in 1899 Aguinaldo broke it into guerrilla bands, and the war changed shape. American soldiers could no longer tell a farmer from a fighter, so they began treating whole towns as the enemy, burning villages, moving civilians into camps, and torturing prisoners for information. Aguinaldo was captured in March 1901. Roosevelt declared the war over on July 4, 1902. Roughly 4,300 Americans and 20,000 Filipino soldiers were dead, along with something near 200,000 civilians, most of them from disease and hunger.

The Major Players

Click a face. Two of them are on the same side and do not agree.

William McKinley

President of the United States

President from 1897. He went to war with Spain over Cuba and came out of it holding a colony on the other side of the world, which he had not planned for and could not easily explain. Eleven days after buying the islands he ordered American rule extended over all of them and called it benevolent assimilation, a phrase built to make an occupation sound like a favor. He was shot in Buffalo in September 1901 and died eight days later, without seeing the end of the war he had started.

Theodore Roosevelt

Rough Rider, then President

He led the Rough Riders in Cuba in 1898 and came home famous, then became governor of New York, then vice president, then president when McKinley was killed. He believed a nation went soft without a fight and that running an empire was proof a people still had spine. In Chicago in April 1899, two months into the fighting, he told an audience that most Filipinos were unfit to govern themselves and that walking away would be cowardice. On July 4, 1902 he declared the war finished and issued an amnesty. Fighting in the southern islands went on for another eleven years.

Mark Twain

Writer, and the war’s loudest critic

The most famous writer in America. He had supported the war against Spain when he believed it was about freeing Cuba, and he turned on it hard once it became a war to keep the Philippines. In February 1901 he published a satire in the North American Review accusing the United States of robbing a trusting friend of his land and his liberty, and of sending its own young men to do bandit work. He served as a vice president of the Anti-Imperialist League of New York until his death in 1910.

Emilio Aguinaldo

President of the Philippine Republic

Born in Cavite in 1869, he was a town mayor at twenty five when he joined the Katipunan, the secret society that rose against Spanish rule in 1896. He was a good enough commander that within a year he was leading the revolution. In 1897 he accepted a truce and went into exile in Hong Kong, paid by Spain to put down his arms. The Americans brought him back in May 1898 aboard one of Dewey’s ships. He raised an army again, took most of Luzon, surrounded Manila, and on June 12, 1898 declared the Philippines independent. In January 1899 he was sworn in as president of the first republic in Asia. When the Americans refused to leave he fought them in the open and lost almost every battle, so he broke his army into guerrilla bands and kept the war going for two more years while moving constantly through the mountains of northern Luzon. He was taken at Palanan in March 1901 by American officers who walked into his camp disguised as prisoners of war, escorted by Filipino scouts working for the United States. He swore allegiance to the United States that April.

The Anti-Imperialist League

The opposition

Founded in 1898 to stop the annexation. Its members argued that a republic built on the consent of the governed could not hold a colony by force and still be a republic. Andrew Carnegie, Jane Addams, and Samuel Gompers all signed on, which tells you how strange a coalition it was. On February 6, 1899 the Senate ratified the Treaty of Paris and took the Philippines, and the League lost by a single vote. It kept publishing for twenty years and never won.

The Argument

Roosevelt and Twain were both Americans, both famous, both writing in the same three years about the same islands. They did not disagree about the facts. They disagreed about which question mattered.

Keep them

Theodore Roosevelt

A nation that refuses a hard job goes soft. Governing the Philippines is a duty America is capable of and the Filipinos are not, and walking away would be cowardice dressed up as principle.

Many of their people are utterly unfit for self-government, and show no signs of becoming fit. Others may in time become fit but at present can only take part in self-government under a wise supervision, at once firm and beneficent.

Speech to the Hamilton Club, Chicago, April 10, 1899

Underneath: some peoples are ready to govern themselves and some are not, and Americans can tell which is which.

Let them go

Mark Twain

The United States told the Filipinos it had come to free them, fought beside them, and then bought the islands from Spain and kept them. Whatever the reasons, the thing itself was theft.

we have robbed a trusting friend of his land and his liberty; we have invited our clean young men to shoulder a discredited musket and do bandits’ work under a flag which bandits have been accustomed to fear, not to follow

To the Person Sitting in Darkness, The North American Review, February 1901

Underneath: whether Filipinos were ready is beside the point, because a promise was made in public and then broken.

So Notice that they are not answering each other. Roosevelt is arguing about capacity, whether Filipinos could run a country. Twain is arguing about honesty, whether America kept its word. Decide which of those is the question that actually settles it, and be ready to say why the other one does not.

Timeline

  1. May 1, 1898Manila BayDewey destroys the Spanish fleet in a morning. Spain is finished in the Pacific.
  2. June 12, 1898Independence declaredAguinaldo proclaims the Philippines free. American officers are present and say nothing.
  3. August 13, 1898Manila fallsSpain surrenders the city to the Americans by arrangement. Filipino troops are kept outside.
  4. December 10, 1898Treaty of Paris signedSpain hands over the Philippines. The United States pays twenty million dollars.
  5. December 21, 1898Benevolent assimilationMcKinley extends US military rule over every island in the group.
  6. January 5, 1899Aguinaldo answersFrom Malolos he calls it a seizure and says his government will fight.
  7. February 4, 1899The shooting startsAn American sentry fires on Filipino soldiers outside Manila. The war is on.
  8. February 6, 1899The Senate buys the islandsThe Senate approves the Treaty of Paris by one vote past the two thirds needed. That vote is what makes the purchase of the Philippines legal under American law.
  9. November 27, 1900IgbarasThe water cure is administered to the town presidente. Igbaras is burned the same night.
  10. March 23, 1901Aguinaldo capturedTaken at Palanan by Americans disguised as prisoners of war.
  11. August 21, 1901The teachers landSix hundred American schoolteachers arrive in Manila while the war is still being fought.
  12. April 1902The Senate hears the soldiersMen who served testify under oath about torture. The country argues about it for months.
  13. July 4, 1902Roosevelt declares it overAn amnesty is issued. Fighting in the southern islands continues to 1913.
  14. July 4, 1946IndependenceThe United States finally recognizes the republic Aguinaldo declared in 1898.

Two Ways to Win

These two things were done by the same government, in the same islands, at the same time.

By force

1899 to 1902

  • Once Aguinaldo broke his army into guerrilla bands, American soldiers could not tell a fighter from a farmer. They began treating whole towns as the enemy, and in some provinces ordered civilians into camps so the countryside could be swept as hostile ground.
  • The water cure was the interrogation method they became known for. Soldiers held a prisoner on his back, forced his mouth open, and poured salt water in until his stomach swelled, then pressed or struck it to force the water out. It was repeated until he talked.
  • At Igbaras in November 1900 the town presidente was given the water cure in front of roughly eighty soldiers, supervised by a US Army judge advocate. The town, four to five hundred houses, was burned to the ground that night.
  • In April 1902 soldiers testified about all of it under oath before the Senate. Governor William Taft conceded that torture had been used on some occasions to extract information.

Captain Edwin Glenn was court martialed over Igbaras. He never denied it happened. He argued it was a legitimate exercise of force under the laws of war, justified by military necessity.

By attraction

1901 to 1902

  • The Education Act of 1901 built a public school system across the islands and made it free.
  • Roughly six hundred American teachers sailed from San Francisco on the army transport Thomas and landed in Manila that August. Filipinos called them the Thomasites.
  • They were 346 men and 180 women, drawn from 43 states and nearly 200 colleges. Most were in their twenties.
  • English became the language of instruction, which is why the Philippines is an English speaking country today.

Americans called this the policy of attraction. The schools were real, the teachers meant it, and the war was still being fought while they taught.

So One reading is that the army and the teachers were two different policies, and the good one eventually won. Another is that they were one policy with two hands, and the schools were how you hold a country once the burning stops. Pick the reading you can defend.
